title: E Major Piano Chord (E): Notes, Inversions & PDF
description: Find E major on piano: E, G-sharp and B. See the keyboard positions, compare E/G-sharp and E/B, and print a three-position reference.
user_task: Locate this exact triad and compare its three bass positions.
questions: Does E mean E major or E minor?
Why is E/B still E major?

blocks.heading: Notes and keyboard position
blocks.body: The E major chord uses E, G-sharp and B. G-sharp is the major third above E; B is the perfect fifth. The displayed root-position example is E4–G♯4–B4. Numbers after note letters identify octaves, not fingers. Use the diagram, note list and bass label together; Play chord sounds the selected notes together, while the note-by-note control sounds them from low to high.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] rules; [推断] register and original teaching example

blocks.heading: What to notice
blocks.body: The triad has one black key, G-sharp. The key signature of E major contains more sharps, but a chord symbol E does not ask you to play all the notes of that scale. It names this particular three-note chord. E to G-sharp is four semitones; E to B is seven. G-sharp and A-flat can share a piano key, but G-sharp is the third-letter spelling above E. An E major triad is therefore written E–G♯–B, not E–A♭–B.
blocks.evidence_status: [推断] original explanation from preserved note data and cited rules

blocks.heading: Compare three positions
blocks.body: Read each bass note before selecting a position. The root-position example starts with E; first inversion starts with G♯; second inversion starts with B. The chord tones stay the same. These are independently chosen reference registers, not an ascending exercise. Switching a position must update the selected note order, diagram, sound and current-print snapshot together. Hand numbers, when available, apply only to the root example.
blocks.evidence_status: [推断] derived inversion explanation; controls are implementation acceptance requirements
